title: CFM, SCFM, ACFM: The Compressed-Air Units That Aren't Interchangeable
h1: CFM, SCFM and ACFM — compressed air and process flow
description: ACFM is actual volumetric flow at line conditions; SCFM normalises to standard T and P. At 100 psig, 1 ACFM ≈ 7.8 SCFM.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: SCFM = ACFM × (P_actual/P_std) × (T_std/T_actual). Miss the correction and compressor sizing overshoots by 30%.
body: Air is compressible, so a volumetric flow rate is meaningless without stating the temperature and pressure it was measured at. SCFM fixes those reference conditions; ACFM lets them float; plain CFM is ambiguous.

> SCFM = ACFM × (P_actual / P_std) × (T_std / T_actual)
> Standard varies by industry: ASME uses 14.7 psia, 68 °F. CAGI uses 14.5 psia, 68 °F, 0% RH. ISO 1217 uses 1 bar, 20 °C, 0% RH.
SCFM: compressor ratings, plant air budgets, sizing calcs. ACFM: fan curves, blower selection, actual duct velocity, filtration face velocity. Nm³/h and Sm³/h: European equivalents.

A tool spec calls for 15 SCFM at 90 psig. At 90 psig line pressure, 15 SCFM = ~2.3 ACFM. Size the drop hose for 2.3 CFM at line pressure, not 15 — velocity and pressure drop drop into spec instead of choking the tool.
'SCFM' varies with the reference standard. Compare specs by the underlying (P, T) — a 15 SCFM (CAGI) rating is ~0.5% different from 15 SCFM (ASME).
Absolute pressure × volumetric flow is the invariant. SCFM is normalised; ACFM is what actually flowed.

faqs.q: Are Nm³/h and SCFM the same?
faqs.a: Same idea, different units. Nm³/h uses 0 °C, 1.01325 bar (or 1 bar in ISO). Convert with the ratio 1 Nm³/h ≈ 0.589 SCFM.
For precise work, yes — water vapour displaces air. CAGI and ISO use 0% RH; ambient air at 50% RH is ~1% lower dry-air density.
